heading: What is principal component analysis?
lead: A way to describe data with fewer features than it was collected with, by finding the directions in which it spreads the most and keeping only those.
points: The problem: real data has many related features. Height and weight, or marks in maths and physics, move together, so two columns carry less than two columns' worth of information.
The idea: rotate the axes so the first new axis points along the greatest spread, the second along the next, and so on. Each new axis is a principal component.
The result: drop the components with the least spread. The data is smaller, and most of what it said is still there.

callout.small: In this example, two features become one and 75% of the variance is kept

notes: PCA finds new axes along the spread of the data and keeps only the ones that matter. Nothing is invented: the new features are combinations of the old ones.

heading: Why use it
points: Fewer features: models train faster and overfit less when correlated columns are replaced by a few uncorrelated ones.
Plots you can read: hundreds of dimensions become two, so clusters and outliers become visible.
Noise falls away: the components with the least variance are usually measurement noise, and dropping them cleans the data.
No labels needed: it works on the data alone, so it is a first step before any supervised model.
You can say what was lost: the eigenvalues state exactly how much variance each component carries, so the trade-off is a number, not a guess.

callout.small: The eigenvalues add up to the total variance, so the share kept is always known

notes: The advantages follow from the eigenvalues: they rank the directions and measure what each one carries, which is what makes the reduction honest.
